question.text: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2+2x_2^2+2x_3^2+6x_1x_2.$
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 2-\lambda & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] (2-\lambda)\begin{vmatrix} 2-\lambda & 3 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] (2-\lambda) \big( (2-\lambda)(2-\lambda) - 9 \big) &= 0 \\[5pt] (2-\lambda) (\lambda^2 - 4\lambda - 5) &= 0 \\[5pt] (2-\lambda) (\lambda - 5)(\lambda + 1) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 5, \, 2, \, -1 \end{align*}

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

\[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 5& 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

\[ 5y_1^2 + 2y_2^2 - y_3^2. \]

question.text: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(\mathbf{x})=7x_1^2+8x_2^2+5x_3^2-4x_2x_3.$

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 7-\lambda & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8-\lambda & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] (7-\lambda)\begin{vmatrix} 8-\lambda & -2 \\ -2 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] (7-\lambda) \big( (8-\lambda)(5-\lambda) - 4 \big) &= 0 \\[5pt] (7-\lambda) (\lambda^2 - 13\lambda + 36) &= 0 \\[5pt] (7-\lambda) (\lambda - 4)(\lambda -9) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 9, \, 7, \, 4 \end{align*}

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

\[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 9& 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

\[ 9y_1^2 + 7y_2^2 + 4y_3^2. \]

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=9x_1^2+4x_1x_2+6x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 9-\lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 6-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2-15\lambda+50 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 10, \, 5 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-6x_1x_2+9x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix}1 - \lambda & -3 \\ -3 & 9 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2-10\lambda&= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 10, \, 0 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -9 & -3 \\ -3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} =- \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\sqrt10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-4x_1x_2-x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} -1-\lambda & -2 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2+2\lambda-3 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 1, \, -3 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 1 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} - 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-3) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} - (-3) \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+12x_1x_2-4x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & 6 \\ 6 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2+3\lambda-40 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 5, \, -8 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-8,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-8) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} - (-8) \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=14x_1^2-6x_1x_2+6x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -3 \\ -3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 14-\lambda & -3 \\ -3 & 6-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2-20\lambda +75 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 15, \, 5 \end{align*}

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=15,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 15 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 15 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-15I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 &-3 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text:
\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=10, \quad$ $\lambda_2=1, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt 5,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = 1,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_3=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt 5,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3 }{\| \mathbf{v}_3 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 5} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0& 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=5, \quad$ $\lambda_2=1, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 1 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = 1,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} =\dfrac{1}{1} \ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_3=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt5,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3 }{\| \mathbf{v}_3 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}&0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=5, \quad$ $\lambda_2=1, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 5\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. % = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = 1,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_3=-1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-1) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} - (-1) \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt 2,$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3 }{\| \mathbf{v}_3 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \]
